slides: Let's continue, with items that repeat.

slides.say: Now items that repeat. Four different letters, A, B, C and D, can stand in four factorial orders, twenty-four.
But what about A, A, A and B? Let's list them.
at: what about A, A, A and B

slides.say: The B can be last, third, second or first. A A A B, A A B A, A B A A, and B A A A. Only four.
Why so few? Let's give the As names for a moment, A one, A two and A three. Now they are four different letters, with twenty-four orders.
But look at these six orders. A one, A two, A three, B. Then A one, A three, A two, B, and so on.
When we take the names off, all six are the same word, A A A B. Swapping the As changes nothing.
at: all six are the same word

slides.say: Six is three factorial, the orders of the three As.
So every word was counted six times. Twenty-four divided by six is four.
Now a new example. A, A, B and B.

Four letters, twenty-four orders, as if all were different. The two As repeat, so we divide by two factorial. The two Bs repeat, so we divide by two factorial again. Twenty-four divided by four is six.
Let's list them to check. A A B B, A B A B, A B B A, B A A B, B A B A and B B A A. Six.
So for repeated items, count as if all were different, then divide by the factorial of each repeat.
And the last rule, a round table. Three people, A, B and C, sit around a round table.
at: Three people, A, B and C

slides.say: In a row, A B C and B C A are different. But at a round table, B C A is the same seating, just turned. Everyone has the same neighbours.
at: B C A is the same seating

slides.say: So A B C, B C A and C A B are one seating. And A C B, C B A and B A C are another.
Three factorial is six rows, but only two seatings.
The trick is to fix one person. A sits in a seat. Then the others fill the remaining seats in two factorial ways, two.
So n people around a table can sit in n minus one, factorial, ways.
For example, five people around a table. Four factorial, twenty-four.
So let's sum it up. Together, glue them into a block, and then multiply by the order inside.
Apart, take all minus together, or use the gaps.
Repeats, divide by the factorial of each repeat.
And a round table is n minus one, factorial. Take a moment to memorize this, and I'll see you in the next video.
